paras: The attempted lynching of McCarthy by Fort Concho soldiers took place on the night of February 1, 1881, when armed Black soldiers from Fort Concho, Texas, went into San Angelo to seize McCarthy, a white man accused of killing a Black cavalryman, William Watkins. They surrounded a hotel and held the sheriff, but McCarthy had been hidden, and they returned when an officer of the guard arrived. The wire carried the story nationally as a foiled lynching, and later Texas reports described shooting into the town and state troops sent.

According to a Fort Concho dispatch to the Dallas Daily Herald, McCarthy shot Watkins, a 10th Cavalry soldier, in the head outside a San Angelo saloon at about 1 a.m. on February 1, then was stopped by a sentinel and held by the post guard. The correspondent called Watkins "a very peaceful negro," described McCarthy as a stranger from Paint Rock, and gave no motive.
The Herald called it "Another murder" of a 10th Cavalry soldier; the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman said a gambler had killed a white soldier from the fort a week earlier and escaped.

On the afternoon of February 1 the military turned McCarthy over to Sheriff Spears, and General Grierson placed a guard around the garrison. A roll call soon after taps showed "a large body of men" absent with arms taken from the racks, and an officer and detachment were sent after them.

The soldiers had surrounded the hotel of Ernest Memittes in San Angelo, demanding McCarthy. They took Sheriff Spears into custody to learn where McCarthy was, but he had been "secreted." When the officer of the guard arrived they returned quietly, "offering no injury to any one," the Herald's correspondent wrote. The wire version said that had they found McCarthy "they would have lynched him."

After a preliminary hearing on February 2, McCarthy was held under strong guard in the county jail at Ben Ficklin. A San Antonio dispatch of February 5 then reported that the previous night soldiers had riddled the Nimitz hotel with bullets, wounded a citizen, and fired into other buildings, seeking McCarthy's life.

The Statesman, citing a Mr. Bentley, reported that the soldiers also demanded McCarthy in the courthouse at his preliminary trial and warned Justice Russell that if bail were allowed they would kill him "and others and burn the town." It added that they spread "incendiary" circulars and that many women and children left. A Frontier Battalion company under Captain Marsh arrived and quiet was restored, and Governor Roberts ordered state troops to Fort Concho. No report of McCarthy's trial or of any punishment of the soldiers appears in the coverage.

The Dallas Daily Herald broke the story on February 2 as "A Negro Soldier Shot and Killed." Its February 3 special was headed "Negro Soldiers at Concho on the Rampage," yet its correspondent hoped the affair would check the shooting of soldiers "by men who think it an act of bravado." On February 4 a two-sentence wire ran in Sacramento as "Seeking Vengeance," in Gold Hill and Salt Lake City, and in Las Vegas as "Ineffectual Lynching." A longer St. Louis wire ran in the New-York Tribune as "Soldiers Intent on Lynching," in the Washington Evening Star as "Colored Lynchers Foiled," and in the Memphis Daily Appeal under the slur "Mokes After McCarthy."

Later Texas reports turned against the soldiers; the Herald's February 6 dispatch, headed "Outrageous Action of Negro Soldiers," said the "good citizens of San Angelo" bore no responsibility for the killings. By February 17 a weekly summary in the Morris Tribune said the soldiers had killed a citizen, which no Texas report stated.

The Herald's February 3 special said the soldiers injured no one, while the Statesman said about 150 soldiers fired some 150 shots into the hotel and houses the night after the killing. The San Antonio dispatch placed the shooting on a later night, possibly a second raid. The Herald's correspondent wrote locally the next day; the Statesman's version came secondhand days later.
The papers also differ on McCarthy, a stranger from Paint Rock in the Herald and a well-to-do sheep raiser of Concho county in the Statesman.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of McCarthy by Fort Concho soldiers
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Armed Black soldiers from Fort Concho went into San Angelo to seize and, by the papers' account, lynch McCarthy, a white man held for killing a Black soldier, but did not find him (A2, A5, A10).

A large body of soldiers acting without authority sought McCarthy to punish him for killing their comrade Watkins, but he had been hidden and was not harmed (A2, A4, A10); the only death in the episode was Watkins, shot by one man, apart from one unsupported summary claim of a citizen killed (A1, A14).

The Dallas Herald's Fort Concho correspondent, the St. Louis wire, and the Austin Statesman's informant all report soldiers going into San Angelo to demand McCarthy (A2, A5, A13), though they disagree on whether shots were fired.

accounts.label: St. Louis / Fort Concho wire
accounts.gist: Comrades of Watkins surrounded the hotel demanding McCarthy, who was not there; a guard took them away; they would have lynched him had they found him.

accounts.label: San Antonio dispatch (via Captain Merritt)

accounts.label: Mr. Bentley, via the Austin Statesman
accounts.gist: About 150 soldiers demanded McCarthy, fired about 150 shots into the hotel and houses, demanded him again at his preliminary trial, threatened Justice Russell and the town, and spread incendiary circulars.

accounts.label: Weekly news summary
accounts.gist: The soldiers attacked the town 'with deadly effect' and one citizen was killed.

framing.detail: The Dallas Herald headlined 'Negro Soldiers at Concho on the Rampage', yet its correspondent called the soldiers 'quiet but determined' and hoped the affair would check the shooting of soldiers 'by men who think it an act of bravado'.
National papers ran the wire as 'Soldiers Intent on Lynching', 'Colored Lynchers Foiled', 'Ineffectual Lynching', and, in Memphis, 'Mokes After McCarthy'.
Later Texas reports called the soldiers' action 'outrageous', stressed that San Angelo citizens were not responsible, and spoke of seeking redress from the United States.
